bull_bear.body: Cash **rose to ₹529bn** (₹390bn free) despite a loss quarter — the defining strength. Deployment is deliberately long-dated: aircraft and engine ownership through GIFT City, land for a unified campus, and the CFM engine-MRO platform. Total debt including capitalised leases ₹815bn against ROU assets ₹553bn. No buyback or dividend discussion. The strategic logic is consistent: **use balance-sheet strength to internalise cost lines (ownership, MRO) that are otherwise USD-linked and escalating.**
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body:
1. **Fuel is uncapped and re-accelerating.** Management entered Q2 expecting relief (*"Going in, we had anticipated Q2 is going to be better than Q1"*) and now says *"if the war kind of starts and... the Hormuz canal, etcetera, is kind of blocked, we may see similar levels of Q1."* MOPAG today ~$140–150.
2. **The domestic ATF cap is gone** (post-9 June). Q2 has no policy cushion — the entire quarter is at market.
3. **Yield-led model has an unknown ceiling.** Loads already −1.3pts. Management refuses to name the fuel level at which fares can no longer keep up.
4. **CASK ex-fuel ex-forex guidance was raised** to possibly low-double-digits — structural, not transitory (FX, gratuity run-rate, contractual escalations).
5. **Deferred senior-management increments are a timing benefit only** — reassessed in six months; the cost returns.
6. **Volume growth ~1%** — IndiGo is currently a price story, not a growth story. The FY28–30 mid-teens capacity plan requires the demand elasticity to survive permanently higher fares.
7. **Airport operators reportedly being permitted to enter the airline business** — MD Rahul Bhatia's response was pointed: *"it has no global precedents because it typically would reflect a massive conflict of interest. And over a period of time, it would actually be against the interest of consumers."* A genuine structural risk to the sector's competitive framework; management is watching, not acting.
8. **CEO transition mid-crisis** — Willie Walsh joins first week of August, into the worst cost environment in years.
9. **Middle East capacity remains hostage to events**, currently "north of 90%" but re-flaring.
10. **Q2 is seasonally weak *and* deliberately shrunk** — the >25% PRASK guide is the only thing standing between flat capacity and another loss.
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: Genuinely strong disclosure quality on the thing that mattered: the CFO walked through the fuel-CASK bridge **three separate times** to three analysts, naming the cap mechanics, the March reference, the VAT/excise layer, the private-supplier gap and the international/domestic blend, and effectively confirmed the analysts' back-solved **₹140–150/litre**. He also volunteered the **ex-currency near-breakeven** framing rather than hiding behind FX, corrected the supplementary-rental base effect unprompted, and **declined three separate invitations to guide** (spread, Q2 fuel, yield ceiling) rather than fabricate. Tone is chastened but not defensive — *"We were hoping that this is behind us... We've recently started to see some flare-up"* and *"Just the very first quarter itself has kind of turned on us."* The MD's contribution was strategic and brief. Notably, **not one long-term target was walked back**, which is either conviction or a reckoning deferred.
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body:
- **The diagnosis has flipped.** FY26's losses were FX-driven with a healthy underlying business (₹75bn underlying PAT). Q1FY27 is the opposite: **FX was almost benign (₹82cr) and the business itself barely broke even.** That is a materially worse quality of loss.
- **Cracks, not crude, broke the quarter.** Brent +50% but **SingJet +120%** — models keyed to Brent will systematically understate airline cost. The CFO said outright that Brent *"is not the right reference point."*
- **The fuel cap was fully passed to consumers**, which means IndiGo captured **none** of the subsidy — and equally faces **no clawback**. Both halves of that are underappreciated.
- **Fuel consumption per ASK was flat** — every efficiency initiative (parking CEOs, OptiClimb) is still ahead of the P&L, not in it.
- **The CFM MoU is a cost-structure move disguised as a fleet announcement**: 1,000+ engines is the volume that justifies building **captive engine MRO and material services**, attacking the maintenance/supplementary-rental line that just normalised 11% higher on FX.
- **May 2026 was the Indian domestic industry's best month ever**, with IndiGo carrying **10mn+ domestic passengers in one month** — demand is not the problem; the cost base is.
- **Post-COVID precedent explicitly invoked**: yields stepped up 40–45% and *stayed*, after which growth reverted to volume. Management is betting on the same pattern — *"As things moderate, we will look towards again, bringing more volume."* The 300bn-ASK/FY30 plan depends on this price level sticking.
- **Damp leases are the swing capacity instrument**: all 13 returned in Q1, decision to re-hire deferred to Q3. This makes Q3 capacity — and therefore FY27 single-digit ASK growth — a live, observable decision point rather than a plan.

bull_bear.body:
- Fuel and energy price shock driven by geopolitical conflict — Conflicts in West Asia have raised crude oil prices and increased freight and insurance costs; IMF estimates project headline inflation rising to 4.4% in CY 2026 with energy prices up 19% and oil prices up 21.4% on production and logistics disruptions. Fuel is the largest swing item in an airline's cost base.
- Airspace closures and route disruption from geopolitical events — During FY 2026 geopolitical developments led to closure of airspace at Pakistan and the Middle East, forcing re-routing, longer flight durations, elevated fuel consumption, higher operating costs and in some cases service cancellations.
- Operational resilience and single-event disruption risk — The Company experienced a brief period of unforeseen and unprecedented operational disruption in early December 2025 that inconvenienced customers, employees and partners, for which the Board issued a formal apology - evidence that a concentrated network can be disrupted at scale by a single event.
- Service-quality and customer-grievance escalation — Customer complaints filed during FY 2026 rose to 44,729 from 1,803 in FY 2025 under the BRSR grievance disclosure, a step-change that carries brand, regulatory and compensation consequences for an airline whose franchise rests on reliability.
- Leadership transition and key-person dependence — The BRSR notes that Mr. Pieter Elbers, Chief Executive Officer, resigned from his services effective 10th March 2026, and the KMP composition disclosed as on 31st March 2026 excludes him - a senior-leadership gap during a phase of international scale-up.
- Global macroeconomic downside and capital-flow volatility — Under an adverse scenario of sustained energy price shocks the IMF sees global growth slowing to 2.5% in CY 2026 with inflation at 5.4%, and to around 2% with inflation above 6% by CY 2027 in a severe scenario, with emerging economies hit nearly twice as hard; conflicts in West Asia have also contributed to volatility in capital flows.
- Climate and aviation-emissions regulation — IndiGo is tracking global climate regulations such as CORSIA, ReFuelEU and the UK RTFO and is preparing to meet applicable compliances; Sustainable Aviation Fuel is being deployed only on flights returning from the EU and UK, and the Indian SAF supply ecosystem is still being developed with regulators and Oil Marketing Companies.
- Structural exposure to a single business line — Scheduled and charter air services for passengers and cargo accounted for 97.35% of turnover per the BRSR, leaving the Company with no meaningful earnings diversification away from air transport cycles.

latest_quarter.body:
**The fuel bridge (management's own decomposition of the +63% QoQ fuel CASK):**
1. **A high base**: March was already elevated (SingJet ~low-80s in Jan, ~82 Feb, then a March spike) and **March became the reference price** for the capped domestic formula.
2. **Domestic was capped, but at +25% over that elevated March reference**, from 1 April to 8 June, courtesy of a government/OMC intervention — *plus VAT and excise on top*.
3. **International was never capped** — full market MOPAG, which ran **+120% vs March**, touching **$180–200**.
4. **Private fuel suppliers largely did not moderate**, pricing at market.
5. **From 9 June the domestic cap lapsed** and everything reverted to MOPAG.
→ Blended Q1 ATF ≈ **₹140–150/litre** vs ~₹85–90 pre-war. Brent **+50% YoY**; **cracks rose far more than Brent** — the crack spread, not crude, is the swing factor. **Fuel burn per ASK was unchanged** — *"there's no change on a per ASK basis as far as the consumption is. Only driver of change has been the rate."*

**The cap was passed through, not pocketed.** Management confirmed the OMC/government support was converted into a **lower fuel charge for domestic passengers**, and that **April–8 June bills have been settled** on the agreed 25%-cap formula — hence **no expected retrospective compensation liability**. They also noted **nobody signed up to the (compensation) scheme because ATF had fallen below the threshold levels** at the time.

**Non-fuel inflation (+11% CASK ex-fuel ex-forex):** (a) **rupee down >11% YoY** on a >50%-USD cost base, (b) **lower utilisation** shrinking the ASK denominator, (c) **annual contractual escalations**. Controllable offsets deployed: **prioritise fuel-efficient aircraft, park older CEOs, tighten discretionary spend, defer senior-management increments**, and pilot **SITA OptiClimb** (AI flight-profile fuel optimisation).

**The pricing philosophy, stated plainly:** Q1 saw **yields +21% against costs +30%+** — the gap *is* the margin collapse. Forward, *"We'll again need to keep testing high levels of yields to offset that increased cost... this is a very dynamic situation. There's nothing that is what we can state that this is it."*

outlook.body:
- Treat the next decade as the most significant phase of international expansion in the company's history, investing in fleet, technology, infrastructure, digital capabilities and talent to build a truly global aviation network originating from India and to establish India as one of the most important global aviation hubs.
- Progressively shift the fleet ownership mix towards owned or finance-leased aircraft, moving from roughly 20% of the current 400+ aircraft fleet to around 30-40% of a projected 600-aircraft fleet by 2030.
- Extend long-haul international operations - launched services to the UK and Eastern Europe, inducted India's first Airbus A321XLR, opened direct connectivity to Athens, became the first Indian carrier to connect India directly with Siem Reap, resumed mainland China operations, and added Kolkata-Shanghai, Delhi-Colombo, Delhi-Krabi and Mumbai-Fujairah.
- Deepen the domestic network as India's largest carrier - 97 destinations and over 520 direct city pairs, with presence across metros and tier 2 and tier 3 markets, and launch-carrier status at Navi Mumbai International Airport and Noida International Airport.
- Build India-based maintenance self-reliance through a world-class MRO facility at Kempegowda International Airport, Bengaluru, expected to be operational in 2028, alongside existing MRO facilities in Delhi and Bengaluru.
- Pursue an AI-first, technology-led operating model - 6Eskai, automation-led initiatives, migration of AMOS to a cloud-based environment, Digi Yatra integration, and a digital travel ecosystem extending into hotels, cabs and travel experiences.
- Scale the IndiGo BluChip loyalty franchise, whose membership base grew to over 11 million during the year.
- Segment the product proposition through the '6E Ways to Fly' framework - Saver, Flexi, UpFront, IndiGoStretch and IndiGoStretch+ - expanding premium offerings while remaining anchored in affordable, on-time, hassle-free travel.
- Keep safety non-negotiable and central to plans, processes and strategies, backed by continued investment in automation, training and process efficiency.
- Invest in people and culture - capability development, leadership programmes, internal mobility and diversity, having crossed 1,000 female pilots with women at 17.4% of the pilot workforce.
- Grow CarGo operations as trade, commerce and time-sensitive logistics expand.
- Sustain a young, fuel-efficient fleet as the core of the decarbonisation approach - average fleet age of 4.9 years, roughly 81% next-generation aircraft, GHG intensity of 60.5 gCO2e/ASK and around 86% of the fleet (excluding wet-lease) compliant with ICAO Chapter 14 noise standards.
- The Dividend Distribution Policy, framed under the Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI LODR, sets out the Board's intent to reward shareholders while maintaining a strong financial position to meet strategic objectives and maintaining reasonably conservative net leverage. Dividend for any period is determined by the Board after considering the Company's financial performance, the advice of executive management and the policy parameters; the Board may decline to declare or recommend a dividend where it considers it prudent to conserve capital for ongoing or planned business expansion or other factors. Parameters considered include annual profit after tax and distributable reserves, cash flow and free cash available, capital allocation plans (investments required to execute strategy, expected working capital and capital expenditure requirements, funds for acquisitions or investment opportunities approved by the Board, any share buy-back plans, and minimum cash for contingencies), funds required to service outstanding debt, liquidity, leverage and return ratios, covenants under financing arrangements with lenders, overall financial position and past dividend trend including any interim dividend. Governance philosophy is anchored on integrity, transparency, accountability and ethical conduct, with a Code of Conduct for Directors and Senior Management and a separate Code of Conduct for all employees; the Board's stated commitments include transparent procedures, full regulatory compliance, timely disclosure of financial and operational information, and independence in reviewing and approving corporate strategy and business plans.
- Decarbonisation anchored on next-generation aircraft: 51 new Airbus A320neo Family aircraft inducted during FY 2026, and next-generation aircraft (including wet-leased) accounted for 81% of the total fleet as of March 2026; these are 15% more fuel-efficient than previous-generation aircraft.
- GHG emission intensity of 60.5 grams of CO2e per Available Seat Kilometre for FY 2026, representing an 18.9% reduction from the 2016 baseline.
- Sustainable Aviation Fuel deployed on flights returning from the EU and UK, with active engagement with Indian regulators and Oil Marketing Companies to support development of a national SAF roadmap and supply ecosystem.

outlook.body: Expansion in FY 2026 was delivered almost entirely through fleet induction and network reach rather than fixed plant. IndiGo continued to expand, strengthen and modernise its fleet with the induction of 51 new fuel-efficient Airbus neo aircraft powered by CFM LEAP-1A engines, taking the fleet as of March 31, 2026 to 177 Airbus A320neo, 168 Airbus A321neo, 1 Airbus A321 XLR, 26 Airbus A320 CEO, 46 ATR aircraft and 3 A321 passenger-to-freighter aircraft, supplemented by damp-leased capacity of 5 Boeing 737, 6 Boeing 787, 5 Airbus A320 CEO and 4 Airbus A321 neo aircraft that provided operational flexibility and capacity support during the year. The company welcomed India's first Airbus A321 XLR for direct long-haul flights and enhanced global connectivity. Network reach expanded to 144 destinations, including 98 domestic and 46 international, with peak operations reaching 2,348 daily flights (2,338 commercial, 6 charter and 4 cargo). Aircraft acquisition is being channelled through the wholly owned financing arm, InterGlobe Aviation Financial Services IFSC Private Limited, established as a unit within the International Financial Services Centre at GIFT City, Gujarat: during FY 2026 it leased a total of 45 aircraft to the Company under operating and financial lease arrangements, and as on March 31, 2026 the total fleet owned by IndiGo IFSC comprised 78 aircraft and 2 landing gears. During FY 2026 IndiGo made an investment of USD 820 million in IndiGo IFSC through a combination of equity shares and Optionally Convertible Redeemable Preference Shares for the purpose of acquisition of aviation assets. A separate venture-investment channel was opened through InterGlobe Aviation Ventures LLP, which acts as Investment Manager to InterGlobe Aviation Ventures, a SEBI-registered Category II Alternate Investment Fund; its first scheme, IndiGo Ventures Fund - I, targets early-stage startups in aviation, aerospace and allied sectors, achieved its first close on July 1, 2025 and made three investments up to March 31, 2026. outlook.body:
- Indian aviation remains structurally underpenetrated - domestic seats per capita of 0.14 versus 3.1 in the US and 0.45 in Vietnam, international at 0.07 versus 0.98 in the US, and only around 8.7% of Indians holding passports, highlighting substantial headroom for growth.
- Expanding middle-class population, rising urbanisation, improving affordability and a growing frequent-flyer base from Tier-II and Tier-III cities support sustained domestic traffic and better capacity utilisation.
- A growing global Indian diaspora of over 35 million underpins year-round VFR-led international demand, enabling higher frequencies on long-haul and regional routes beyond seasonal peaks.
- Demographic dividend - the working-age population (20-59) is expected to rise from 53% in 2015 to 57% in 2030, and by 2036 India's middle class and affluent consumers are expected to account for 93% of all spending.
- Easier international travel for Indian citizens through visa relaxation, e-visa and visa-on-arrival, improved bilateral air service agreements and digital processes reduces travel friction.
- Medical and wellness tourism is a structural international demand driver, with revenues projected to grow from USD 18.2 billion in 2025 to USD 58.2 billion by 2035 at a 12.3% CAGR; spiritual and religious tourism adds non-cyclical, year-round domestic demand.
- Large-scale airport infrastructure build-out - operational airports rose from 74 in 2014 to over 160 in 2025, and the Airports Authority of India will invest Rs. 15,000 crore by 2028 to upgrade ATC tower automation and navigational systems.
- Secondary airports are emerging as growth drivers by decongesting saturated metro hubs, supporting point-to-point connectivity and creating new international gateways.
- Regional connectivity policy support - the Modified UDAN Scheme for FY 2027 to FY 2036 carries an outlay of Rs. 28,840 crore, aiming to develop 100 airports, support operations at about 441 aerodromes and provide Rs. 10,043 crore of viability gap funding over 10 years.
- India's geographic position between Europe, Southeast Asia and Australia supports development of hub-based transit networks, while wide-body deployment on long-haul routes reduces dependence on foreign hubs.
- A strengthening domestic MRO ecosystem, supported by government policy, can lower maintenance costs and reduce reliance on foreign MROs; Safran Aircraft Engine Services India is setting up its first aircraft engine OEM MRO facility in India.
- Near-term demand is muted - in FY 2026 Indian domestic passenger traffic grew only 1.1% against seat growth of 2.6%, and international passenger traffic grew 3.3% against seat growth of 4.6%.
- Industry supply remains constrained by supply-side challenges, engine reliability issues and large order backlogs, which continue to limit airlines' expansion plans globally.
- Fuel remains a significant component of airline operating costs and an important margin driver; airlines are responding with calibrated fare increases, fuel surcharges and capacity rationalisation on underperforming routes.
- Global passenger traffic is expected to increase by only 2.1% year-on-year in CY 2026 with a negative bias from geopolitical uncertainty and supply-chain challenges, with Africa leading at 10%.
- Air cargo demand is expected to keep growing in CY 2026 but at a more moderate rate than CY 2025, with growth increasingly driven by volume rather than price, particularly in Asia and Europe.
- The FY 2027 Indian aviation outlook is highly sensitive to geopolitical uncertainty, intermittent airspace restrictions that raise international route costs, and volatility in crude oil prices and exchange rates.
- Forward fleet pipeline is framed qualitatively as a projected 600-aircraft fleet by 2030 versus the current 400+ aircraft; no aircraft order-book quantum or delivery schedule is disclosed in the routed sections.
- Industry-wide, capacity expansion remains constrained by supply-side challenges, engine reliability issues and large order backlogs.

deepdive.thesis: The fare engine worked and the fuel line still swamped it. IndiGo pushed **yields +21.3%** and **PRASK +19%** — comfortably ahead of the mid-teens it guided in May — yet **fuel CASK rose ~80% YoY and ~63% QoQ**, dragging EBITDAR margin from **28% to 15.6%** and producing a **₹2.4bn net loss**. The tell is the ex-currency number: **a net loss of just ₹56mn**, versus ₹23bn profit a year ago — this is a *fuel* quarter, not an FX quarter, a reversal of FY26's diagnosis. Management's response is textbook: shrink capacity into the weak quarter (**Q2 flattish**), price harder (**Q2 PRASK >25%**), park old CEO aircraft, return damp leases, defer senior-management increments. The uncomfortable admission is that the yield lever is now uncapped and reactive — *"we'll have to keep testing higher levels of yields also just to offset the increased cost"* — with no target spread and no visibility, because the Middle East conflict, which management believed was closing at end-June, **has flared up again**. Every long-dated commitment (single-digit FY27 ASK, mid-teens FY28–30, 40% international by 2030, 300bn ASK by FY30) was nonetheless **explicitly reaffirmed**.

IndiGo continued to expand, strengthen and modernise its fleet with the induction of 51 new fuel-efficient Airbus neo aircraft powered by CFM LEAP-1A engines, taking the fleet as of March 31, 2026 to 177 Airbus A320neo, 168 Airbus A321neo, 1 Airbus A321 XLR, 26 Airbus A320 CEO, 46 ATR aircraft and 3 A321 passenger-to-freighter aircraft, supplemented by damp-leased capacity of 5 Boeing 737, 6 Boeing 787, 5 Airbus A320 CEO and 4 Airbus A321 neo aircraft that provided operational flexibility and capacity support during the year. The company welcomed India's first Airbus A321 XLR for direct long-haul flights and enhanced global connectivity. Network reach expanded to 144 destinations, including 98 domestic and 46 international, with peak operations reaching 2,348 daily flights (2,338 commercial, 6 charter and 4 cargo). Aircraft acquisition is being channelled through the wholly owned financing arm, InterGlobe Aviation Financial Services IFSC Private Limited, established as a unit within the International Financial Services Centre at GIFT City, Gujarat: during FY 2026 it leased a total of 45 aircraft to the Company under operating and financial lease arrangements, and as on March 31, 2026 the total fleet owned by IndiGo IFSC comprised 78 aircraft and 2 landing gears. During FY 2026 IndiGo made an investment of USD 820 million in IndiGo IFSC through a combination of equity shares and Optionally Convertible Redeemable Preference Shares for the purpose of acquisition of aviation assets. A separate venture-investment channel was opened through InterGlobe Aviation Ventures LLP, which acts as Investment Manager to InterGlobe Aviation Ventures, a SEBI-registered Category II Alternate Investment Fund; its first scheme, IndiGo Ventures Fund - I, targets early-stage startups in aviation, aerospace and allied sectors, achieved its first close on July 1, 2025 and made three investments up to March 31, 2026. risks.risk: Fuel and energy price shock driven by geopolitical conflict
risks.note: Conflicts in West Asia have raised crude oil prices and increased freight and insurance costs; IMF estimates project headline inflation rising to 4.4% in CY 2026 with energy prices up 19% and oil prices up 21.4% on production and logistics disruptions. Fuel is the largest swing item in an airline's cost base.

risks.risk: Airspace closures and route disruption from geopolitical events
risks.note: During FY 2026 geopolitical developments led to closure of airspace at Pakistan and the Middle East, forcing re-routing, longer flight durations, elevated fuel consumption, higher operating costs and in some cases service cancellations.

risks.risk: Operational resilience and single-event disruption risk
risks.note: The Company experienced a brief period of unforeseen and unprecedented operational disruption in early December 2025 that inconvenienced customers, employees and partners, for which the Board issued a formal apology - evidence that a concentrated network can be disrupted at scale by a single event.

Customer complaints filed during FY 2026 rose to 44,729 from 1,803 in FY 2025 under the BRSR grievance disclosure, a step-change that carries brand, regulatory and compensation consequences for an airline whose franchise rests on reliability.

The BRSR notes that Mr. Pieter Elbers, Chief Executive Officer, resigned from his services effective 10th March 2026, and the KMP composition disclosed as on 31st March 2026 excludes him - a senior-leadership gap during a phase of international scale-up.

risks.risk: Global macroeconomic downside and capital-flow volatility
risks.note: Under an adverse scenario of sustained energy price shocks the IMF sees global growth slowing to 2.5% in CY 2026 with inflation at 5.4%, and to around 2% with inflation above 6% by CY 2027 in a severe scenario, with emerging economies hit nearly twice as hard; conflicts in West Asia have also contributed to volatility in capital flows.

IndiGo is tracking global climate regulations such as CORSIA, ReFuelEU and the UK RTFO and is preparing to meet applicable compliances; Sustainable Aviation Fuel is being deployed only on flights returning from the EU and UK, and the Indian SAF supply ecosystem is still being developed with regulators and Oil Marketing Companies.

risks.risk: Structural exposure to a single business line
risks.note: Scheduled and charter air services for passengers and cargo accounted for 97.35% of turnover per the BRSR, leaving the Company with no meaningful earnings diversification away from air transport cycles.

one-line thesis: The fare engine worked and the fuel line still swamped it. IndiGo pushed **yields +21.3%** and **PRASK +19%** — comfortably ahead of the mid-teens it guided in May — yet **fuel CASK rose ~80% YoY and ~63% QoQ**, dragging EBITDAR margin from **28% to 15.6%** and producing a **₹2.4bn net loss**. The tell is the ex-currency number: **a net loss of just ₹56mn**, versus ₹23bn profit a year ago — this is a *fuel* quarter, not an FX quarter, a reversal of FY26's diagnosis. Management's response is textbook: shrink capacity into the weak quarter (**Q2 flattish**), price harder (**Q2 PRASK >25%**), park old CEO aircraft, return damp leases, defer senior-management increments. The uncomfortable admission is that the yield lever is now uncapped and reactive — *"we'll have to keep testing higher levels of yields also just to offset the increased cost"* — with no target spread and no visibility, because the Middle East conflict, which management believed was closing at end-June, **has flared up again**. Every long-dated commitment (single-digit FY27 ASK, mid-teens FY28–30, 40% international by 2030, 300bn ASK by FY30) was nonetheless **explicitly reaffirmed**.

margins & cost dynamics:
**The fuel bridge (management's own decomposition of the +63% QoQ fuel CASK):**
1. **A high base**: March was already elevated (SingJet ~low-80s in Jan, ~82 Feb, then a March spike) and **March became the reference price** for the capped domestic formula.
2. **Domestic was capped, but at +25% over that elevated March reference**, from 1 April to 8 June, courtesy of a government/OMC intervention — *plus VAT and excise on top*.
3. **International was never capped** — full market MOPAG, which ran **+120% vs March**, touching **$180–200**.
4. **Private fuel suppliers largely did not moderate**, pricing at market.
5. **From 9 June the domestic cap lapsed** and everything reverted to MOPAG.
→ Blended Q1 ATF ≈ **₹140–150/litre** vs ~₹85–90 pre-war. Brent **+50% YoY**; **cracks rose far more than Brent** — the crack spread, not crude, is the swing factor. **Fuel burn per ASK was unchanged** — *"there's no change on a per ASK basis as far as the consumption is. Only driver of change has been the rate."*

**The cap was passed through, not pocketed.** Management confirmed the OMC/government support was converted into a **lower fuel charge for domestic passengers**, and that **April–8 June bills have been settled** on the agreed 25%-cap formula — hence **no expected retrospective compensation liability**. They also noted **nobody signed up to the (compensation) scheme because ATF had fallen below the threshold levels** at the time.

**Non-fuel inflation (+11% CASK ex-fuel ex-forex):** (a) **rupee down >11% YoY** on a >50%-USD cost base, (b) **lower utilisation** shrinking the ASK denominator, (c) **annual contractual escalations**. Controllable offsets deployed: **prioritise fuel-efficient aircraft, park older CEOs, tighten discretionary spend, defer senior-management increments**, and pilot **SITA OptiClimb** (AI flight-profile fuel optimisation).

**The pricing philosophy, stated plainly:** Q1 saw **yields +21% against costs +30%+** — the gap *is* the margin collapse. Forward, *"We'll again need to keep testing high levels of yields to offset that increased cost... this is a very dynamic situation. There's nothing that is what we can state that this is it."*
capex / expansion (watch slippage):
- **13 aircraft inducted, 4 engines purchased outright**, all via **GIFT City** — continued shift from lease to ownership.
- **Partial payment made for land for the unified campus.**
- **9 original-orderbook aircraft redelivered and 13 damp-leased aircraft returned** — a deliberate fleet contraction into a high-fuel, weak-season environment. Own-fleet plan unchanged; **damp-lease re-hire is a Q3 decision**, explicitly contingent on Middle East de-escalation and fuel moderation.
- **Older CEO-technology aircraft parked** where not commercially justified — instantly reversible capacity.
- **Slippage watch:** Q2 capacity flattish means FY27 single-digit ASK growth needs a strong H2; if Q3 damp leases are *not* taken, the single-digit guide is at risk from below.
capital allocation: Cash **rose to ₹529bn** (₹390bn free) despite a loss quarter — the defining strength. Deployment is deliberately long-dated: aircraft and engine ownership through GIFT City, land for a unified campus, and the CFM engine-MRO platform. Total debt including capitalised leases ₹815bn against ROU assets ₹553bn. No buyback or dividend discussion. The strategic logic is consistent: **use balance-sheet strength to internalise cost lines (ownership, MRO) that are otherwise USD-linked and escalating.**
risks & watch-items:
1. **Fuel is uncapped and re-accelerating.** Management entered Q2 expecting relief (*"Going in, we had anticipated Q2 is going to be better than Q1"*) and now says *"if the war kind of starts and... the Hormuz canal, etcetera, is kind of blocked, we may see similar levels of Q1."* MOPAG today ~$140–150.
2. **The domestic ATF cap is gone** (post-9 June). Q2 has no policy cushion — the entire quarter is at market.
3. **Yield-led model has an unknown ceiling.** Loads already −1.3pts. Management refuses to name the fuel level at which fares can no longer keep up.
4. **CASK ex-fuel ex-forex guidance was raised** to possibly low-double-digits — structural, not transitory (FX, gratuity run-rate, contractual escalations).
5. **Deferred senior-management increments are a timing benefit only** — reassessed in six months; the cost returns.
6. **Volume growth ~1%** — IndiGo is currently a price story, not a growth story. The FY28–30 mid-teens capacity plan requires the demand elasticity to survive permanently higher fares.
7. **Airport operators reportedly being permitted to enter the airline business** — MD Rahul Bhatia's response was pointed: *"it has no global precedents because it typically would reflect a massive conflict of interest. And over a period of time, it would actually be against the interest of consumers."* A genuine structural risk to the sector's competitive framework; management is watching, not acting.
8. **CEO transition mid-crisis** — Willie Walsh joins first week of August, into the worst cost environment in years.
9. **Middle East capacity remains hostage to events**, currently "north of 90%" but re-flaring.
10. **Q2 is seasonally weak *and* deliberately shrunk** — the >25% PRASK guide is the only thing standing between flat capacity and another loss.
management quality / tone: Genuinely strong disclosure quality on the thing that mattered: the CFO walked through the fuel-CASK bridge **three separate times** to three analysts, naming the cap mechanics, the March reference, the VAT/excise layer, the private-supplier gap and the international/domestic blend, and effectively confirmed the analysts' back-solved **₹140–150/litre**. He also volunteered the **ex-currency near-breakeven** framing rather than hiding behind FX, corrected the supplementary-rental base effect unprompted, and **declined three separate invitations to guide** (spread, Q2 fuel, yield ceiling) rather than fabricate. Tone is chastened but not defensive — *"We were hoping that this is behind us... We've recently started to see some flare-up"* and *"Just the very first quarter itself has kind of turned on us."* The MD's contribution was strategic and brief. Notably, **not one long-term target was walked back**, which is either conviction or a reckoning deferred.
non-obvious takeaways:
- **The diagnosis has flipped.** FY26's losses were FX-driven with a healthy underlying business (₹75bn underlying PAT). Q1FY27 is the opposite: **FX was almost benign (₹82cr) and the business itself barely broke even.** That is a materially worse quality of loss.
- **Cracks, not crude, broke the quarter.** Brent +50% but **SingJet +120%** — models keyed to Brent will systematically understate airline cost. The CFO said outright that Brent *"is not the right reference point."*
- **The fuel cap was fully passed to consumers**, which means IndiGo captured **none** of the subsidy — and equally faces **no clawback**. Both halves of that are underappreciated.
- **Fuel consumption per ASK was flat** — every efficiency initiative (parking CEOs, OptiClimb) is still ahead of the P&L, not in it.
- **The CFM MoU is a cost-structure move disguised as a fleet announcement**: 1,000+ engines is the volume that justifies building **captive engine MRO and material services**, attacking the maintenance/supplementary-rental line that just normalised 11% higher on FX.
- **May 2026 was the Indian domestic industry's best month ever**, with IndiGo carrying **10mn+ domestic passengers in one month** — demand is not the problem; the cost base is.
- **Post-COVID precedent explicitly invoked**: yields stepped up 40–45% and *stayed*, after which growth reverted to volume. Management is betting on the same pattern — *"As things moderate, we will look towards again, bringing more volume."* The 300bn-ASK/FY30 plan depends on this price level sticking.
- **Damp leases are the swing capacity instrument**: all 13 returned in Q1, decision to re-hire deferred to Q3. This makes Q3 capacity — and therefore FY27 single-digit ASK growth — a live, observable decision point rather than a plan.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: IndiGo (InterGlobe Aviation) is India's largest and most preferred airline and one of the fastest-growing carriers worldwide, built on affordable, on-time, hassle-free air travel delivered through a large standardised fleet and a low-cost operating model.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: InterGlobe Aviation operates scheduled passenger and cargo air services under the IndiGo brand across an extensive network spanning key economic hubs and emerging regional markets in India and internationally, covering 144 destinations (98 domestic and 46 international) in FY 2026. Since inception in 2006 the airline has grown on the back of a robust, largely Airbus narrow-body fleet, outstanding aircraft utilisation and a cost-efficient approach, serving leisure, business and VFR travellers alongside charter and air-cargo customers. Ground handling is delivered in-house through a wholly owned subsidiary, and aircraft financing and leasing is routed through a wholly owned IFSC-based financing arm.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Indian aviation remains structurally underpenetrated - domestic seats per capita of 0.14 versus 3.1 in the US and 0.45 in Vietnam, international at 0.07 versus 0.98 in the US, and only around 8.7% of Indians holding passports, highlighting substantial headroom for growth.
- Expanding middle-class population, rising urbanisation, improving affordability and a growing frequent-flyer base from Tier-II and Tier-III cities support sustained domestic traffic and better capacity utilisation.
- A growing global Indian diaspora of over 35 million underpins year-round VFR-led international demand, enabling higher frequencies on long-haul and regional routes beyond seasonal peaks.
- Demographic dividend - the working-age population (20-59) is expected to rise from 53% in 2015 to 57% in 2030, and by 2036 India's middle class and affluent consumers are expected to account for 93% of all spending.
- Easier international travel for Indian citizens through visa relaxation, e-visa and visa-on-arrival, improved bilateral air service agreements and digital processes reduces travel friction.
- Medical and wellness tourism is a structural international demand driver, with revenues projected to grow from USD 18.2 billion in 2025 to USD 58.2 billion by 2035 at a 12.3% CAGR; spiritual and religious tourism adds non-cyclical, year-round domestic demand.
- Large-scale airport infrastructure build-out - operational airports rose from 74 in 2014 to over 160 in 2025, and the Airports Authority of India will invest Rs. 15,000 crore by 2028 to upgrade ATC tower automation and navigational systems.
- Secondary airports are emerging as growth drivers by decongesting saturated metro hubs, supporting point-to-point connectivity and creating new international gateways.
- Regional connectivity policy support - the Modified UDAN Scheme for FY 2027 to FY 2036 carries an outlay of Rs. 28,840 crore, aiming to develop 100 airports, support operations at about 441 aerodromes and provide Rs. 10,043 crore of viability gap funding over 10 years.
- India's geographic position between Europe, Southeast Asia and Australia supports development of hub-based transit networks, while wide-body deployment on long-haul routes reduces dependence on foreign hubs.
- A strengthening domestic MRO ecosystem, supported by government policy, can lower maintenance costs and reduce reliance on foreign MROs; Safran Aircraft Engine Services India is setting up its first aircraft engine OEM MRO facility in India.
- Near-term demand is muted - in FY 2026 Indian domestic passenger traffic grew only 1.1% against seat growth of 2.6%, and international passenger traffic grew 3.3% against seat growth of 4.6%.
- Industry supply remains constrained by supply-side challenges, engine reliability issues and large order backlogs, which continue to limit airlines' expansion plans globally.
- Fuel remains a significant component of airline operating costs and an important margin driver; airlines are responding with calibrated fare increases, fuel surcharges and capacity rationalisation on underperforming routes.
- Global passenger traffic is expected to increase by only 2.1% year-on-year in CY 2026 with a negative bias from geopolitical uncertainty and supply-chain challenges, with Africa leading at 10%.
- Air cargo demand is expected to keep growing in CY 2026 but at a more moderate rate than CY 2025, with growth increasingly driven by volume rather than price, particularly in Asia and Europe.
- The FY 2027 Indian aviation outlook is highly sensitive to geopolitical uncertainty, intermittent airspace restrictions that raise international route costs, and volatility in crude oil prices and exchange rates.
- Forward fleet pipeline is framed qualitatively as a projected 600-aircraft fleet by 2030 versus the current 400+ aircraft; no aircraft order-book quantum or delivery schedule is disclosed in the routed sections.
- Industry-wide, capacity expansion remains constrained by supply-side challenges, engine reliability issues and large order backlogs.

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body:
**The fuel bridge (management's own decomposition of the +63% QoQ fuel CASK):**
1. **A high base**: March was already elevated (SingJet ~low-80s in Jan, ~82 Feb, then a March spike) and **March became the reference price** for the capped domestic formula.
2. **Domestic was capped, but at +25% over that elevated March reference**, from 1 April to 8 June, courtesy of a government/OMC intervention — *plus VAT and excise on top*.
3. **International was never capped** — full market MOPAG, which ran **+120% vs March**, touching **$180–200**.
4. **Private fuel suppliers largely did not moderate**, pricing at market.
5. **From 9 June the domestic cap lapsed** and everything reverted to MOPAG.
→ Blended Q1 ATF ≈ **₹140–150/litre** vs ~₹85–90 pre-war. Brent **+50% YoY**; **cracks rose far more than Brent** — the crack spread, not crude, is the swing factor. **Fuel burn per ASK was unchanged** — *"there's no change on a per ASK basis as far as the consumption is. Only driver of change has been the rate."*

**The cap was passed through, not pocketed.** Management confirmed the OMC/government support was converted into a **lower fuel charge for domestic passengers**, and that **April–8 June bills have been settled** on the agreed 25%-cap formula — hence **no expected retrospective compensation liability**. They also noted **nobody signed up to the (compensation) scheme because ATF had fallen below the threshold levels** at the time.

**Non-fuel inflation (+11% CASK ex-fuel ex-forex):** (a) **rupee down >11% YoY** on a >50%-USD cost base, (b) **lower utilisation** shrinking the ASK denominator, (c) **annual contractual escalations**. Controllable offsets deployed: **prioritise fuel-efficient aircraft, park older CEOs, tighten discretionary spend, defer senior-management increments**, and pilot **SITA OptiClimb** (AI flight-profile fuel optimisation).

**The pricing philosophy, stated plainly:** Q1 saw **yields +21% against costs +30%+** — the gap *is* the margin collapse. Forward, *"We'll again need to keep testing high levels of yields to offset that increased cost... this is a very dynamic situation. There's nothing that is what we can state that this is it."*

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation
capital_allocation.body: Cash **rose to ₹529bn** (₹390bn free) despite a loss quarter — the defining strength. Deployment is deliberately long-dated: aircraft and engine ownership through GIFT City, land for a unified campus, and the CFM engine-MRO platform. Total debt including capitalised leases ₹815bn against ROU assets ₹553bn. No buyback or dividend discussion. The strategic logic is consistent: **use balance-sheet strength to internalise cost lines (ownership, MRO) that are otherwise USD-linked and escalating.**

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Expansion in FY 2026 was delivered almost entirely through fleet induction and network reach rather than fixed plant. IndiGo continued to expand, strengthen and modernise its fleet with the induction of 51 new fuel-efficient Airbus neo aircraft powered by CFM LEAP-1A engines, taking the fleet as of March 31, 2026 to 177 Airbus A320neo, 168 Airbus A321neo, 1 Airbus A321 XLR, 26 Airbus A320 CEO, 46 ATR aircraft and 3 A321 passenger-to-freighter aircraft, supplemented by damp-leased capacity of 5 Boeing 737, 6 Boeing 787, 5 Airbus A320 CEO and 4 Airbus A321 neo aircraft that provided operational flexibility and capacity support during the year. The company welcomed India's first Airbus A321 XLR for direct long-haul flights and enhanced global connectivity. Network reach expanded to 144 destinations, including 98 domestic and 46 international, with peak operations reaching 2,348 daily flights (2,338 commercial, 6 charter and 4 cargo). Aircraft acquisition is being channelled through the wholly owned financing arm, InterGlobe Aviation Financial Services IFSC Private Limited, established as a unit within the International Financial Services Centre at GIFT City, Gujarat: during FY 2026 it leased a total of 45 aircraft to the Company under operating and financial lease arrangements, and as on March 31, 2026 the total fleet owned by IndiGo IFSC comprised 78 aircraft and 2 landing gears. During FY 2026 IndiGo made an investment of USD 820 million in IndiGo IFSC through a combination of equity shares and Optionally Convertible Redeemable Preference Shares for the purpose of acquisition of aviation assets. A separate venture-investment channel was opened through InterGlobe Aviation Ventures LLP, which acts as Investment Manager to InterGlobe Aviation Ventures, a SEBI-registered Category II Alternate Investment Fund; its first scheme, IndiGo Ventures Fund - I, targets early-stage startups in aviation, aerospace and allied sectors, achieved its first close on July 1, 2025 and made three investments up to March 31, 2026. The routed sections carry no rupee capex plan or project schedule; industry context notes that capacity expansion across aviation remains constrained by supply-side challenges, engine reliability issues and large order backlogs.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Genuinely strong disclosure quality on the thing that mattered: the CFO walked through the fuel-CASK bridge **three separate times** to three analysts, naming the cap mechanics, the March reference, the VAT/excise layer, the private-supplier gap and the international/domestic blend, and effectively confirmed the analysts' back-solved **₹140–150/litre**. He also volunteered the **ex-currency near-breakeven** framing rather than hiding behind FX, corrected the supplementary-rental base effect unprompted, and **declined three separate invitations to guide** (spread, Q2 fuel, yield ceiling) rather than fabricate. Tone is chastened but not defensive — *"We were hoping that this is behind us... We've recently started to see some flare-up"* and *"Just the very first quarter itself has kind of turned on us."* The MD's contribution was strategic and brief. Notably, **not one long-term target was walked back**, which is either conviction or a reckoning deferred.

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body:
1. **Fuel is uncapped and re-accelerating.** Management entered Q2 expecting relief (*"Going in, we had anticipated Q2 is going to be better than Q1"*) and now says *"if the war kind of starts and... the Hormuz canal, etcetera, is kind of blocked, we may see similar levels of Q1."* MOPAG today ~$140–150.
2. **The domestic ATF cap is gone** (post-9 June). Q2 has no policy cushion — the entire quarter is at market.
3. **Yield-led model has an unknown ceiling.** Loads already −1.3pts. Management refuses to name the fuel level at which fares can no longer keep up.
4. **CASK ex-fuel ex-forex guidance was raised** to possibly low-double-digits — structural, not transitory (FX, gratuity run-rate, contractual escalations).
5. **Deferred senior-management increments are a timing benefit only** — reassessed in six months; the cost returns.
6. **Volume growth ~1%** — IndiGo is currently a price story, not a growth story. The FY28–30 mid-teens capacity plan requires the demand elasticity to survive permanently higher fares.
7. **Airport operators reportedly being permitted to enter the airline business** — MD Rahul Bhatia's response was pointed: *"it has no global precedents because it typically would reflect a massive conflict of interest. And over a period of time, it would actually be against the interest of consumers."* A genuine structural risk to the sector's competitive framework; management is watching, not acting.
8. **CEO transition mid-crisis** — Willie Walsh joins first week of August, into the worst cost environment in years.
9. **Middle East capacity remains hostage to events**, currently "north of 90%" but re-flaring.
10. **Q2 is seasonally weak *and* deliberately shrunk** — the >25% PRASK guide is the only thing standing between flat capacity and another loss.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body:
- **The diagnosis has flipped.** FY26's losses were FX-driven with a healthy underlying business (₹75bn underlying PAT). Q1FY27 is the opposite: **FX was almost benign (₹82cr) and the business itself barely broke even.** That is a materially worse quality of loss.
- **Cracks, not crude, broke the quarter.** Brent +50% but **SingJet +120%** — models keyed to Brent will systematically understate airline cost. The CFO said outright that Brent *"is not the right reference point."*
- **The fuel cap was fully passed to consumers**, which means IndiGo captured **none** of the subsidy — and equally faces **no clawback**. Both halves of that are underappreciated.
- **Fuel consumption per ASK was flat** — every efficiency initiative (parking CEOs, OptiClimb) is still ahead of the P&L, not in it.
- **The CFM MoU is a cost-structure move disguised as a fleet announcement**: 1,000+ engines is the volume that justifies building **captive engine MRO and material services**, attacking the maintenance/supplementary-rental line that just normalised 11% higher on FX.
- **May 2026 was the Indian domestic industry's best month ever**, with IndiGo carrying **10mn+ domestic passengers in one month** — demand is not the problem; the cost base is.
- **Post-COVID precedent explicitly invoked**: yields stepped up 40–45% and *stayed*, after which growth reverted to volume. Management is betting on the same pattern — *"As things moderate, we will look towards again, bringing more volume."* The 300bn-ASK/FY30 plan depends on this price level sticking.
- **Damp leases are the swing capacity instrument**: all 13 returned in Q1, decision to re-hire deferred to Q3. This makes Q3 capacity — and therefore FY27 single-digit ASK growth — a live, observable decision point rather than a plan.

one-line thesis: The fare engine worked and the fuel line still swamped it. IndiGo pushed **yields +21.3%** and **PRASK +19%** — comfortably ahead of the mid-teens it guided in May — yet **fuel CASK rose ~80% YoY and ~63% QoQ**, dragging EBITDAR margin from **28% to 15.6%** and producing a **₹2.4bn net loss**. The tell is the ex-currency number: **a net loss of just ₹56mn**, versus ₹23bn profit a year ago — this is a *fuel* quarter, not an FX quarter, a reversal of FY26's diagnosis. Management's response is textbook: shrink capacity into the weak quarter (**Q2 flattish**), price harder (**Q2 PRASK >25%**), park old CEO aircraft, return damp leases, defer senior-management increments. The uncomfortable admission is that the yield lever is now uncapped and reactive — *"we'll have to keep testing higher levels of yields also just to offset the increased cost"* — with no target spread and no visibility, because the Middle East conflict, which management believed was closing at end-June, **has flared up again**. Every long-dated commitment (single-digit FY27 ASK, mid-teens FY28–30, 40% international by 2030, 300bn ASK by FY30) was nonetheless **explicitly reaffirmed**.

- **Fleet:** **MoU signed with CFM International for 1,000+ LEAP-1A engines**, supporting future deliveries plus development of IndiGo's **own engine MRO and long-term material services**.
- **Explicitly REFUSED to guide:** RASK–CASK spread (*"we can't give you a guidance on the spread right now"*), Q2 fuel cost direction, and any target yield/spread floor (*"there's no kind of a target, but we just want it to be a healthy kind of a spread"*).
order book & pipeline: Aircraft orderbook deliveries **on plan** — 13 inducted in Q1, all through the GIFT City ownership entity. The **CFM MoU for over 1,000 LEAP-1A engines** is the headline forward commitment, notable less for the engines than for what rides on it: **an in-house engine MRO and material-services platform**, i.e. a deliberate move to internalise the maintenance cost line that has been inflating on FX and contractual escalation. A321 XLR and wide-body deliveries are described as on track and are the mechanism for the 40%-international-by-2030 target.
segment / subsidiary detail:
- **Domestic:** the ballast. **May 2026 was the best month ever for the Indian domestic industry**, and IndiGo carried **over 10 million domestic passengers in a single month — its highest ever**. April was weak (disruption + constrained sentiment + network recalibration); June was constructive on yields.
- **International — Middle East:** the Q1 capacity story. Daily departures ran **~150 pre-war → 20–30 at the crisis peak → 130+ by end-June → "north of 90%"** of normal today. Management's posture: *"our intention is to keep operating Middle East till the point it's safe for us to operate at the maximum amount of capacity that we can go to."* **The crisis has re-flared** as of the call.
- **International — East:** the Q2 story, and seasonal rather than geopolitical. **Six eastern destinations moderated**, with **Langkawi, Ho Chi Minh City, Hong Kong and Shanghai suspended, restarting October.**
- **GIFT City entity:** now the sole conduit for asset ownership — all 13 aircraft inductions plus **4 engine purchases** in Q1.
- **Loyalty (BluChip):** **Accor "ALL" partnership went live**, extending earn/burn across hospitality.
- **Network additions:** **Jamnagar** launched; **first airline to operate from Jewar (Noida) airport**, deepening the NCR multi-airport position.
- **Ancillary/product:** **"Lite Fare"** launched for no-check-in-bag travellers with paid add-ons — unbundling revenue without breaking the single-class model.
margins & cost dynamics:
**The fuel bridge (management's own decomposition of the +63% QoQ fuel CASK):**
1. **A high base**: March was already elevated (SingJet ~low-80s in Jan, ~82 Feb, then a March spike) and **March became the reference price** for the capped domestic formula.
2. **Domestic was capped, but at +25% over that elevated March reference**, from 1 April to 8 June, courtesy of a government/OMC intervention — *plus VAT and excise on top*.
3. **International was never capped** — full market MOPAG, which ran **+120% vs March**, touching **$180–200**.
4. **Private fuel suppliers largely did not moderate**, pricing at market.
5. **From 9 June the domestic cap lapsed** and everything reverted to MOPAG.
→ Blended Q1 ATF ≈ **₹140–150/litre** vs ~₹85–90 pre-war. Brent **+50% YoY**; **cracks rose far more than Brent** — the crack spread, not crude, is the swing factor. **Fuel burn per ASK was unchanged** — *"there's no change on a per ASK basis as far as the consumption is. Only driver of change has been the rate."*

**The cap was passed through, not pocketed.** Management confirmed the OMC/government support was converted into a **lower fuel charge for domestic passengers**, and that **April–8 June bills have been settled** on the agreed 25%-cap formula — hence **no expected retrospective compensation liability**. They also noted **nobody signed up to the (compensation) scheme because ATF had fallen below the threshold levels** at the time.

**Non-fuel inflation (+11% CASK ex-fuel ex-forex):** (a) **rupee down >11% YoY** on a >50%-USD cost base, (b) **lower utilisation** shrinking the ASK denominator, (c) **annual contractual escalations**. Controllable offsets deployed: **prioritise fuel-efficient aircraft, park older CEOs, tighten discretionary spend, defer senior-management increments**, and pilot **SITA OptiClimb** (AI flight-profile fuel optimisation).

**The pricing philosophy, stated plainly:** Q1 saw **yields +21% against costs +30%+** — the gap *is* the margin collapse. Forward, *"We'll again need to keep testing high levels of yields to offset that increased cost... this is a very dynamic situation. There's nothing that is what we can state that this is it."*
capex / expansion (watch slippage):
- **13 aircraft inducted, 4 engines purchased outright**, all via **GIFT City** — continued shift from lease to ownership.
- **Partial payment made for land for the unified campus.**
- **9 original-orderbook aircraft redelivered and 13 damp-leased aircraft returned** — a deliberate fleet contraction into a high-fuel, weak-season environment. Own-fleet plan unchanged; **damp-lease re-hire is a Q3 decision**, explicitly contingent on Middle East de-escalation and fuel moderation.
- **Older CEO-technology aircraft parked** where not commercially justified — instantly reversible capacity.
- **Slippage watch:** Q2 capacity flattish means FY27 single-digit ASK growth needs a strong H2; if Q3 damp leases are *not* taken, the single-digit guide is at risk from below.
capital allocation: Cash **rose to ₹529bn** (₹390bn free) despite a loss quarter — the defining strength. Deployment is deliberately long-dated: aircraft and engine ownership through GIFT City, land for a unified campus, and the CFM engine-MRO platform. Total debt including capitalised leases ₹815bn against ROU assets ₹553bn. No buyback or dividend discussion. The strategic logic is consistent: **use balance-sheet strength to internalise cost lines (ownership, MRO) that are otherwise USD-linked and escalating.**
risks & watch-items:
1. **Fuel is uncapped and re-accelerating.** Management entered Q2 expecting relief (*"Going in, we had anticipated Q2 is going to be better than Q1"*) and now says *"if the war kind of starts and... the Hormuz canal, etcetera, is kind of blocked, we may see similar levels of Q1."* MOPAG today ~$140–150.
2. **The domestic ATF cap is gone** (post-9 June). Q2 has no policy cushion — the entire quarter is at market.
3. **Yield-led model has an unknown ceiling.** Loads already −1.3pts. Management refuses to name the fuel level at which fares can no longer keep up.
4. **CASK ex-fuel ex-forex guidance was raised** to possibly low-double-digits — structural, not transitory (FX, gratuity run-rate, contractual escalations).
5. **Deferred senior-management increments are a timing benefit only** — reassessed in six months; the cost returns.
6. **Volume growth ~1%** — IndiGo is currently a price story, not a growth story. The FY28–30 mid-teens capacity plan requires the demand elasticity to survive permanently higher fares.
7. **Airport operators reportedly being permitted to enter the airline business** — MD Rahul Bhatia's response was pointed: *"it has no global precedents because it typically would reflect a massive conflict of interest. And over a period of time, it would actually be against the interest of consumers."* A genuine structural risk to the sector's competitive framework; management is watching, not acting.
8. **CEO transition mid-crisis** — Willie Walsh joins first week of August, into the worst cost environment in years.
9. **Middle East capacity remains hostage to events**, currently "north of 90%" but re-flaring.
10. **Q2 is seasonally weak *and* deliberately shrunk** — the >25% PRASK guide is the only thing standing between flat capacity and another loss.
management quality / tone: Genuinely strong disclosure quality on the thing that mattered: the CFO walked through the fuel-CASK bridge **three separate times** to three analysts, naming the cap mechanics, the March reference, the VAT/excise layer, the private-supplier gap and the international/domestic blend, and effectively confirmed the analysts' back-solved **₹140–150/litre**. He also volunteered the **ex-currency near-breakeven** framing rather than hiding behind FX, corrected the supplementary-rental base effect unprompted, and **declined three separate invitations to guide** (spread, Q2 fuel, yield ceiling) rather than fabricate. Tone is chastened but not defensive — *"We were hoping that this is behind us... We've recently started to see some flare-up"* and *"Just the very first quarter itself has kind of turned on us."* The MD's contribution was strategic and brief. Notably, **not one long-term target was walked back**, which is either conviction or a reckoning deferred.
non-obvious takeaways:
- **The diagnosis has flipped.** FY26's losses were FX-driven with a healthy underlying business (₹75bn underlying PAT). Q1FY27 is the opposite: **FX was almost benign (₹82cr) and the business itself barely broke even.** That is a materially worse quality of loss.
- **Cracks, not crude, broke the quarter.** Brent +50% but **SingJet +120%** — models keyed to Brent will systematically understate airline cost. The CFO said outright that Brent *"is not the right reference point."*
- **The fuel cap was fully passed to consumers**, which means IndiGo captured **none** of the subsidy — and equally faces **no clawback**. Both halves of that are underappreciated.
- **Fuel consumption per ASK was flat** — every efficiency initiative (parking CEOs, OptiClimb) is still ahead of the P&L, not in it.
- **The CFM MoU is a cost-structure move disguised as a fleet announcement**: 1,000+ engines is the volume that justifies building **captive engine MRO and material services**, attacking the maintenance/supplementary-rental line that just normalised 11% higher on FX.
- **May 2026 was the Indian domestic industry's best month ever**, with IndiGo carrying **10mn+ domestic passengers in one month** — demand is not the problem; the cost base is.
- **Post-COVID precedent explicitly invoked**: yields stepped up 40–45% and *stayed*, after which growth reverted to volume. Management is betting on the same pattern — *"As things moderate, we will look towards again, bringing more volume."* The 300bn-ASK/FY30 plan depends on this price level sticking.
- **Damp leases are the swing capacity instrument**: all 13 returned in Q1, decision to re-hire deferred to Q3. This makes Q3 capacity — and therefore FY27 single-digit ASK growth — a live, observable decision point rather than a plan.

themes.title: Hospitality & travel up-cycle
themes.need: Q1FY27 split hotels from airlines. INDHOTEL delivered a 17th consecutive record quarter - consolidated revenue INR 2,419cr (+15%), EBITDA INR 753cr at 31.1%, standalone occupancy jumping to 82% from 76% on a 41.8% standalone EBITDA margin, and asset-light management-fee income INR 168cr (+26%) - with management now framing the West-Asia war as a NET tailwind because outbound travel stays home; leisure RevPAR (Rajasthan/Goa) ran up high-20s. Airlines got the mirror image: INDIGO's EBITDAR margin collapsed from 28.0% to 15.6% on blended ATF of ~INR 140-150/litre versus INR 85-90 pre-war (fuel CASK +~80% YoY), leaving yield as the only defence. MHRIL shows domestic leisure premiumisation is real - Keystone average unit realisation +73% to INR 14.4 lakh on stable gross sales. LEMONTREE/CHALET/SAMHI/THELEELA ride the same occupancy-led room cycle; TRAVELFOOD/TBOTEK/DREAMFOLKS remain levered to airport PAX and B2B travel.
themes.driver: Occupancy-led (not rate-led) RevPAR compounding plus INDHOTEL's Ginger conversion cadence stepping 15->20->25->40 per quarter through FY27; for airlines the swing is INDIGO's guided Q2 PRASK growth of 'more than 25%' on flattish capacity against ATF cracks.
